cards.front: A closer relative is not the same kind. Fungi are closer to animals than to plants. Does that make a mushroom an animal?
cards.back: No. Being a closer relative means sharing a more recent common ancestor, not belonging to the same group. A mushroom is still a fungus.
cards.quote: A closer relative is not the same kind: fungi are closer to animals, but a mushroom is not an animal.

cards.front: Why is one protein match count a clue and not proof of who is most closely related?
cards.back: One group's gene can change faster, so the closest match is not always the closest relative. Scientists want many genes to agree before they trust a grouping.
cards.quote: One match count is a clue, not proof: one group's gene can change faster, so the closest match is not always the closest relative.

cards.front: A {{c1::nucleus}} is the part of a cell that holds its DNA.
cards.quote: A nucleus is the part of a cell that holds its DNA.
cards.section: Explain: six kingdoms inside three domains

cards.front: A {{c1::chloroplast}} is a green part where a cell makes sugar (glucose) using light.
cards.quote: A chloroplast is a green part where a cell makes sugar (glucose) using light.
cards.section: Explain: six kingdoms inside three domains

cards.front: Name the three domains of life.
cards.back: Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya.
cards.quote: Bacteria and Archaea are two domains of tiny, mostly single-celled organisms with no nucleus; they look alike but differ in cell chemistry and genes.
cards.section: Explain: six kingdoms inside three domains

cards.front: How are Bacteria and Archaea different from Eukarya, and how are they different from each other?
cards.back: Bacteria and Archaea cells have no nucleus; Eukarya cells have one. Bacteria and Archaea look alike but differ in cell chemistry and genes.
cards.quote: Eukarya is the domain of all organisms whose cells have a nucleus.
cards.section: Explain: six kingdoms inside three domains

cards.front: In the six kingdoms many US textbooks use, which four kingdoms are inside the domain Eukarya?
cards.back: Protists, fungi, plants and animals. Bacteria and Archaea each get one kingdom of their own.
cards.quote: Many US textbooks use six kingdoms: Bacteria and Archaea each get one, and four are inside Eukarya.
cards.section: Explain: six kingdoms inside three domains

cards.front: What is a protist? Give one example.
cards.back: An organism with a nucleus that is not a plant, animal or fungus. Example: a paramecium.
cards.quote: A protist is an organism with a nucleus that is not a plant, animal or fungus
cards.section: Explain: six kingdoms inside three domains

cards.front: What four clues are used to sort living things into kingdoms, and which one needs more than a microscope?
cards.back: Nucleus or not, which cell parts (cell wall, chloroplasts), one cell or many, and how it gets food. A microscope shows the first three; other tests show how it gets food.
cards.quote: A microscope shows three clues (nucleus, cell parts, one cell or many); other tests add how it gets food.
cards.section: Explain: six kingdoms inside three domains

cards.front: Fungi have cell walls, like plants. Why are fungi not grouped with plants?
cards.back: Fungus cells have no chloroplasts, so they cannot make sugar using light. Fungi take in their food; most plants make theirs.
cards.quote: Fungi separated by how they get food
cards.section: Explain: new tools bring new evidence

cards.front: Baker's yeast is a single cell, like a paramecium. It has a nucleus and a cell wall but no chloroplasts, and it takes in sugar as food. Protist or fungus?
cards.back: A fungus. Being one cell does not make it a protist.
cards.why: Its cell wall, missing chloroplasts and taking in food match the Fungi kingdom.
cards.quote: Baker's yeast is a single cell, like a paramecium.
cards.section: Explain: six kingdoms inside three domains

cards.front: An organism has many cells. Its cells have a nucleus, but no cell wall and no chloroplasts. It takes in its food. Which kingdom fits best?
cards.back: Animals.
cards.why: No cell wall rules out fungi and plants. No chloroplasts and taking in food also rule out plants.
cards.quote: A cell wall is a stiff layer outside the cell membrane.
cards.section: Explain: six kingdoms inside three domains

cards.front: A pond organism is a single cell. It has a nucleus and chloroplasts and makes its own food. Which kingdom fits best: plants, animals, fungi or protists?
cards.back: Protists.
cards.why: Plants have many cells, fungi and animals have no chloroplasts. A one-celled organism with a nucleus that fits none of those is a protist.
cards.quote: such as a paramecium; protists are a mixed group (see Going deeper).
cards.section: Explain: six kingdoms inside three domains

cards.front: Linnaeus used just two kingdoms, plants and animals. What new tool led scientists to add a third kingdom, and what did it show?
cards.back: The microscope. It showed tiny living things that were neither plant nor animal.
cards.quote: Tiny living things that were neither plant nor animal
cards.section: Explain: new tools bring new evidence

cards.front: Bacteria and Archaea look alike under a microscope. What kind of evidence showed that Archaea are a separate main line of life?
cards.back: Comparing sequences: the order of building blocks in a molecule all cells have (ribosomal RNA).
cards.quote: Comparing the sequence of a molecule all cells have (ribosomal RNA)
cards.section: Explain: new tools bring new evidence

cards.front: In the comparison of the protein EF-1 alpha, what does a match percent count?
cards.back: Matching amino acids, the building blocks of a protein. It does not count matching letters in DNA, and it is for one protein, not all of the DNA.
cards.quote: But these percents count matching amino acids, the building blocks of a protein.
cards.section: Elaborate: compare one protein in five organisms

cards.front: For the protein EF-1 alpha, the two animal-and-fungus pairs matched 80.7% and 83.9%. The four fungus-and-plant pairs matched 73.5%, 73.5%, 74.0% and 75.3%. Find each mean. Which is higher, and by about how much?
cards.back: Animal-and-fungus: (80.7 + 83.9) / 2 = 82.3%. Fungus-and-plant: (73.5 + 73.5 + 74.0 + 75.3) / 4 = about 74.1%. Animal-and-fungus is higher by about 8 percentage points.
cards.why: For this one protein, fungi match animals better than plants.
cards.quote: Find the mean match for the two animal-and-fungus pairs.
cards.section: Elaborate: compare one protein in five organisms

cards.front: In the EF-1 alpha table, thale cress and wheat matched best of all pairs, at 95.3%. Why does that make sense?
cards.back: Both are plants, so it makes sense they match most; this is one protein, a clue not proof.
cards.why: Members of the same group probably share a more recent common ancestor.
cards.quote: Thale cress, a small weed used in plant research, and wheat are plants, like the oak.
cards.section: Elaborate: compare one protein in five organisms

cards.front: For EF-1 alpha, bread mold matched the human about 3 percentage points better than baker's yeast did. Is bread mold a closer relative of humans than yeast is?
cards.back: No. Both are fungi, so they are equally related to animals.
cards.why: Yeast's version may simply have changed more; yeast also matches both plants a little less. One protein cannot show the reason.
cards.quote: From the human's side, bread mold matched about 3 percentage points better than baker's yeast.
cards.section: Elaborate: compare one protein in five organisms

cards.front: Bottles of yeast in warm water get 0 grams or 10 grams of sugar, with a balloon on each to catch carbon dioxide. What is the control, and what result would show that yeast takes in sugar?
cards.back: Control: the bottle with yeast and water but no sugar. Larger balloons with sugar would show the yeast takes in sugar and breaks it down.
cards.why: Fungi take in food. Similar balloons would mean the test showed no clear effect of sugar.
cards.quote: Control: the bottle with yeast and water but no sugar.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Which kinds of evidence moved the mushroom out of the plants, and which kind put it beside the animals?
cards.back: Cell clues and feeding (no chloroplasts, takes in food) moved it out of the plants. DNA comparisons put it beside the animals.
cards.why: Cell clues and feeding cannot say who the closest relatives are; comparing genes or proteins can.
cards.quote: Back to the one idea: cell clues and feeding moved the mushroom out of the plants, and the DNA rung put it beside the animals.
cards.section: Evaluate: check your thinking

cards.front: Water molds have the cell clues of a fungus, but DNA shows they are not fungi. What does this show about sorting by cell clues alone?
cards.back: Cell clues can group look-alikes that are not close relatives. DNA evidence can move a living thing to a new group.
cards.quote: Some look-alikes, such as water molds, share the fungus clues, but DNA shows they are not fungi.
cards.section: Going deeper
